subject: Accounting
title: Payroll Taxes
description: A fast breakdown of Payroll Taxes for builders.

hook.text: Before your paycheck reaches you, payroll taxes take a bite—funding Social Security and Medicare.

buildup.text: Employers and employees each pay 7.65% of wages. Self-employed workers pay both halves.

discovery.text: Social Security tax applies only up to a wage cap—about $168,600 in 2024.

twist.text: Someone earning $170,000 and someone earning $10 million pay the same Social Security tax.

climax.text: Payroll taxes are the second-largest source of federal revenue, right behind income tax.

punchline.text: Everyone pays payroll tax. The cap decides who stops.

details.summary: Payroll taxes are levied on wages and salaries to fund Social Security and Medicare, split between employer and employee contributions. They are the second-largest federal revenue source and affect every working American.
details.whyItMatters: Payroll taxes directly reduce take-home pay for every worker and fund the social safety net programs that most Americans will eventually rely on, making them crucial to understand.
takeaways: Payroll taxes fund Social Security (6.2% each from employer and employee) and Medicare (1.45% each)
These taxes are regressive — Social Security tax stops at a wage cap while Medicare applies to all earnings
Payroll taxes are the second-largest source of federal revenue after individual income taxes

faq.question: How much do payroll taxes cost?
faq.answer: Employees pay 7.65% of wages (6.2% Social Security plus 1.45% Medicare), and employers match that amount for a combined 15.3%. Self-employed individuals pay the full 15.3%. Social Security tax applies only up to a wage cap ($168,600 in 2024), while Medicare has no cap.

faq.question: Why are payroll taxes considered regressive?
faq.answer: Social Security tax only applies up to a wage cap, so high earners pay a smaller percentage of total income than lower earners. Someone earning $170,000 and someone earning $1,700,000 pay the same dollar amount in Social Security tax, making it proportionally lighter for the wealthy.
